turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Um, well, I guess my manager actually kind of pushed me to come in, because things have just been getting really... difficult at work lately. I'm a hairstylist, and usually, you know, it's a really fast-paced environment. You have to stay on schedule, get people in and out, sweep up, do the consultations. But lately, I don't know how to explain it other than my hands just feel like they’re moving through actual glue. Like, thick glue. 

Every single physical thing I do takes so much effort. Even just the really basic stuff that I could normally do in my sleep, like parting and sectioning a client's hair before a cut, or going to the back room to mix up a bowl of color... it takes me forever now. I'll be standing there with the developer and the color tubes, and my arms just feel so incredibly heavy, like I'm moving in slow motion or underwater or something. 

And the worst part is that people have definitely started noticing. My coworkers are having to sweep my station for me, and my manager pulled me aside the other day because I’m just so much slower than I used to be. Even a couple of my regular clients were kind of looking at me funny in the mirror because it took me an extra twenty minutes just to do a basic root touch-up. It's just so frustrating because I know what I'm doing, I went to school, I got my associate's, I know all the techniques, but my body just won't cooperate and I just keep dragging through every single appointment, and I don't know why I can't just move at a normal speed anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient describes feeling like her hands are moving through glue, her arms feeling heavy, moving in slow motion, and being noticeably slower at physical tasks, which indicates psychomotor retardation.

turns.doctor_question: Along with this feeling of being physically slowed down, how has your overall mood been lately?
turns.patient_response:
Well, honestly... it's just been awful. Just really, really awful. It's not just the moving slow, it's... it's like this constant, heavy, flat sadness that just sits right in the middle of my chest. Most days, I wake up and before I even open my eyes, I can feel it there, just pressing down on me. And I just lay in bed staring at the ceiling, thinking, what is even the point? 

I used to have all these plans, you know? Like, I got my associate's, I got my chair at the salon, and I was going to build up this huge clientele and maybe open my own studio one day. I had this whole vision board on my phone with, like, the aesthetics of the salon I wanted, and the types of color correction I wanted to specialize in. But now... now I just look at it and feel absolutely nothing. Well, not nothing, but just this deep, heavy sadness. It's like the color has been completely drained out of everything. 

I try to shake it off, I really do. I'll put on my favorite playlist on my drive to the salon, the one that usually gets me pumped up for the day, but it just sounds like noise. And then I get to work, and I have to put on this fake smile for my clients and pretend everything is fine, but inside, I'm just drowning in this feeling that there's no point in trying to build the life I was planning. It's just so exhausting to feel this sad all the time, on top of feeling like my body is made of lead. It's just... it's too much.

turns.doctor_question: About how long have you been feeling this heavy sadness and slowness?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... it's been a really long time. I mean, the heavy depression, that feeling of just being completely weighed down and hollowed out, it's been with me for about a year and two months now. I remember because it started right around the time the salon had its big holiday party last year, which was, you know, early December. I had actually bought this really pretty velvet dress for it months in advance, back when I still cared about that sort of thing, and I remember putting it on and just looking in the mirror and feeling absolutely nothing but this crushing weight in my chest. 

I ended up not even going. I just sat on the edge of my bed for hours. And since then, it's just been this constant companion. A year and two months of waking up every single day and having to fight just to get out from under the covers. And the slowness, the feeling like I'm moving through wet cement, that kind of crept in along with it and just kept getting worse. Like, at first, I thought maybe I was just tired from the holiday rush at the salon, because November and December are always our busiest months, you know? Everyone wants their color touched up before Thanksgiving and Christmas. But then January came, and February, and the rush was over, but I was still dragging. 

And it's just never stopped. For fourteen whole months, I've been dragging myself through every single haircut, every single highlight, every single day, just feeling so incredibly sad and so incredibly slow. It feels like a lifetime, honestly. I look back at pictures of myself from before, like from Halloween last year, and I don't even recognize that girl anymore. It's just been a year and two months of feeling like a completely different, broken version of myself, and I just don't know how much longer I can keep pushing through it like this.

symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient describes a persistent lack of energy, noting she has to 'fight just to get out from under the covers' and is constantly 'dragging' herself through the day.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period of time where you felt the exact opposite of this—unusually energetic, needing very little sleep, or feeling like your thoughts were racing?
turns.patient_response:
No, never. I mean, I can't even imagine feeling like that right now. The idea of having too much energy? Or not needing sleep? That sounds like a completely different person. I sleep all the time, or at least I try to, because being awake is just so exhausting. 

Even back before all this started, when I was feeling normal, I was never like... hyper, you know? I was just a regular twenty-year-old girl. I liked my sleep. I'd sleep in until noon on my days off if I didn't have plans. I mean, sure, there were times at the salon where we'd be slammed, like on a Saturday before prom season, and I'd be running on iced coffee and adrenaline, just bouncing from chair to chair, doing an updo here, a blowout there. But that was just normal busy-ness, you know? It wasn't like I was buzzing out of my skin or my brain was going a million miles an hour for no reason. 

And as soon as my shift was over, I would crash. Hard. I'd go home, order takeout, and pass out on the couch watching reality TV. I never had a time where I just didn't need to sleep for days on end, or where I felt like I was on top of the world for no reason. Honestly, I've always been pretty even-keeled. Maybe a little anxious sometimes about building my clientele, but never that crazy, racing-thoughts kind of energy you're talking about. It's always just been either normal, or now... this. Just this heavy, slow, awful feeling. So no, definitely nothing like that.

turns.doctor_question: Before this started about fourteen months ago, had you ever gone through another period in your life where you felt depressed or down like this?
turns.patient_response:
No, I... I really don't think so. I mean, I've had bad days, obviously. Everyone has bad days, right? Like, I remember back in high school, when I didn't make the cheer squad my junior year, I was pretty devastated. I cried for, like, three days straight and refused to come out of my room. My mom had to practically drag me out of bed to go to school that Monday. But that was just normal high school drama, you know? It wasn't this... this sickness. 

And then there was the time right after I graduated with my associate's degree, before I got hired at the salon. I was applying everywhere, dropping off my resume, doing trial cuts, and just getting rejected or ghosted. I felt really discouraged then. I started doubting if I even picked the right career path, if I was actually any good at hair, or if I just wasted all that time and money on school. I'd sit on my couch eating ice cream and watching old episodes of America's Next Top Model, just feeling sorry for myself. 

But even then, it wasn't like this. I could still laugh at a joke, I could still get out of bed, I still wanted to talk to my friends. If my best friend called and said, "Hey, let's go get coffee," I would go, and I would actually enjoy the coffee. But this... what I've been feeling for the last year and two months... it's completely different. It's not just feeling sad because something bad happened. It's like my brain is just broken. So, no, before all this started fourteen months ago, I had never, ever felt anything even close to this level of just... absolute darkness. It's completely new, and it's completely terrifying.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes their current state over the past fourteen months as a 'sickness' characterized by 'absolute darkness,' confirming a severe depressed mood.
symptom_reasoning.S025: By contrasting their past ability to laugh, socialize, and enjoy things like getting coffee with their current state ('But this... is completely different'), the patient strongly implies current anhedonia, social withdrawal, and loss of motivation.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed yourself feeling unusually sensitive to the cold, or feeling chilly even when other people are comfortable?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm always a little bit cold, but that's just because I'm small, you know? And the salon is always freezing. They keep the AC blasting all year round because the blow dryers and the flat irons generate so much heat, and if they don't keep it cool, the stylists who are running around all day start sweating, and nobody wants their hairstylist sweating on them while they're getting a blowout. 

So I've always brought a cardigan to work. I have this really soft, oversized gray one that I keep draped over my chair in the breakroom, and I usually throw it on between clients. But it's not like I'm sitting there shivering when everyone else is fine. And at home, I just keep the thermostat where I always have, around 70 or 71. I haven't had to crank it up to 80 or anything crazy like that. 

I mean, honestly, most of the time I'm just bundled up in blankets anyway, but that's not because I'm physically cold. It's more of a... a comfort thing, I guess? Or just a hiding thing. When I'm under the covers, the world feels a little bit smaller and a little less overwhelming. I'll just pull my big down comforter all the way up to my chin and lie there for hours. But if you're asking if I'm physically freezing all the time, no, not really. Just the normal amount of chilly you get from sitting still for too long or being in a drafty room. Nothing unusual.
